Crazy
KRAY-zee
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From craze (to crack, to shatter), a Middle English word probably of Scandinavian origin; so crazy first meant cracked or full of flaws, then broken in mind, and Webster gave both senses in 1828. Jazz musicians turned it around by the late 1920s to mean exciting, wonderful; by the 1950s the bop and beat crowd said crazy, man, crazy for anything they liked.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In a 1950s coffeehouse, if a fellow played a wild saxophone solo, someone would say, "Crazy, man." It meant great. The older meaning was not great at all: cracked, broken, out of one’s right mind. The slang turned a sorrow into a compliment, and there is a strange truth in that, because the world has always called God’s best things crazy. Paul wrote that "the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God" (1Co 1:18). When Paul preached the resurrection before a Roman governor, Festus shouted, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). Paul answered, "I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness" (Act 26:25). The gospel sounds crazy to the world because it is truer than the world. And Christ is the One who heals real madness. The man of the Gadarenes, wild among the tombs, was found "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mar 5:15). That is what Jesus does: "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). So the Christian should be gentle with the word. Real affliction of the mind is suffering, not a joke, and those who bear it deserve our kindness. And the Christian should not mind being called crazy for Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (jazz from the late 1920s; bop and beat 1950s) for exciting, wonderful — a reversal of the 1828 sense of cracked or deranged, as the world calls the preaching of the cross foolishness (1Co 1:18).

expand to see more

CRAZY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz use from the late 1920s) Excellent, exciting, wonderful. "Crazy, man, crazy!"

Webster (1828) — CRAZY, adjective 1. Broken; decrepit; weak; feeble; applied to the body, or constitution, or any structure; as a crazy body; a crazy constitution; a crazy ship. 2. Broken, weakened, or disordered in intellect; deranged, weakened, or shattered in mind. We say, the man is crazy

Decode for families: in the coffeehouse, crazy meant great; in the Bible, the world calls the gospel crazy, and Christ gives a sound mind.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:18 — "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God."

Act 26:24 — "And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad."

Act 26:25 — "But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness."

Mar 5:15 — "And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid."

2Ti 1:7 — "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind."

Modern Corruption

The jazz compliment is harmless; the care Scripture asks is not to make light of real affliction of the mind, and not to fear being called crazy for the gospel.

expand to see more

Crazy as praise did no harm in 1955 and does none now. The word does carry an older weight. For most of its history it named a real and painful thing, and children should learn not to mock anyone who suffers in mind. Christ met such sufferers with compassion and healing (Mar 5:15), and so should His people.

The other lesson runs the opposite way. The world has always judged the gospel to be madness (1Co 1:18; Act 26:24). A Christian should expect it, answer with "truth and soberness" as Paul did, and not be ashamed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English crasen (to crack, shatter) → crazy (cracked; deranged) → late-1920s jazz (exciting, wonderful) → 1950s bop and beat crazy, man.
